::: {.lead}
A game is built from code, but the player meets it through its media: the
characters they see, the music they hear, the lines of dialogue they read and
the cut-scenes they watch. This course is about those media — how they are
written, designed, recorded, edited and protected. This first chapter defines
digital media, explains how sound and pictures become numbers, describes the
game as a medium that combines all other media, and outlines the production
process that turns an idea into finished game content.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary digital-media digitization raster-image vector-graphics multimedia elemental-tetrad mechanics aesthetics player-experience asset production-pipeline pre-production >}}

## 1.1 What digital media are

A **medium** (plural *media*) is a form through which content is communicated:
writing, pictures, sound, moving images. **Digital media** are media whose
content is encoded as numbers, so that a computer can store, edit, copy and
transmit it. The main types of digital media used in games are:

- **text** — dialogue, item descriptions, menus, subtitles;
- **images** — characters, backgrounds, icons, textures;
- **audio** — music, sound effects, voices, ambience;
- **video** — cut-scenes, trailers, recorded gameplay;
- **animation** — sequences of images or poses that create motion;
- **interactive media** — content that responds to the user, of which the
  game itself is the most complete example.

A work that combines several of these types is called **multimedia**.

### How sound and pictures become numbers

Sound and light in the real world are *continuous*: a sound wave varies
smoothly in time, and a scene varies smoothly in space. A computer can only
store a finite list of numbers. The conversion, called **digitization**, has
two steps (@fig-sampling):

1. **sampling** — measuring the signal at regular intervals (in time for
   sound, in space for an image);
2. **quantization** — rounding each measurement to one of a fixed number of
   levels.

![Digitizing a sound wave: the continuous signal is sampled at regular times, and each sample is rounded to the nearest level.](images/sampling.png){#fig-sampling width=86%}

The number of samples per second is the **sample rate**, measured in hertz;
the number of bits used for each sample is the **bit depth**. Audio CDs use
44 100 samples per second and 16 bits per sample. For an image, the samples
are pixels: the **resolution** gives their number and the colour depth gives
the bits per pixel. With 8 bits for each of red, green and blue (24 bits per
pixel), a pixel can take $2^{24} \approx 16.7$ million colours.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Size of uncompressed media"}
Uncompressed audio needs
$\text{sample rate} \times \text{bit depth} \times \text{channels}$ bits per
second. An uncompressed image needs
$\text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{bits per pixel}$ bits.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — Why media must be compressed"}
1. One second of CD-quality stereo audio:
   $44\,100 \times 16 \times 2 = 1\,411\,200$ bits $\approx 176$ KB.
   A 3-minute music track: $176 \times 180 \approx 31.8$ MB.
2. One uncompressed frame of full-HD video ($1920 \times 1080$, 24 bits):
   $1920 \times 1080 \times 3$ bytes $\approx 6.2$ MB. At 30 frames per second,
   one second of video needs about 187 MB.
3. These sizes are far too large for a mobile game. Formats such as MP3 and
   Ogg Vorbis for audio, PNG and JPEG for images and H.264 for video
   **compress** the data, often to a tenth of its size or less; weeks 7 and 11
   study them.
:::

Images can also be stored in a completely different way. A **raster** (or
bitmap) image is a grid of pixels; it is ideal for photographs and painted
art, but becomes blocky when it is enlarged. A **vector** image stores shapes
— lines, curves and fills described by coordinates — and is redrawn at any
size without loss; it suits logos, icons and interface elements
(@fig-raster-vector).

![The same icon as a raster image (left, enlarged: the pixels become visible) and as vector graphics (right, sharp at any size).](images/raster-vector.png){#fig-raster-vector width=80%}

## 1.2 Properties of digital media

Because they are numbers, digital media behave differently from paint on
canvas or sound on tape. Following the media theorist Lev Manovich, five
properties can be distinguished; each has a direct consequence for games.

| Property | Meaning | In games |
|---|---|---|
| numerical representation | the content is numbers, so it can be computed | colours, volumes and positions are changed by code at runtime |
| modularity | a work is assembled from independent parts | a level is built from reusable sprites, tiles, sounds and models |
| automation | parts of creation can be done by programs | procedural levels, generated terrain, automatic lip-sync |
| variability | one work can exist in many versions | music that adapts to danger; skins; translations |
| transcoding | content moves between the computer's logic and human culture | game data are both art for the player and files for the engine |

: Properties of digital media and their effect on games (after Manovich). {#tbl-props}

A sixth property is central to this course: **interactivity**. A film is the
same at every viewing; a game changes its images and sounds in response to the
player. Game media must therefore be designed not as one fixed sequence but
as a *set of possibilities*: a sound effect may play once or a hundred times,
a line of dialogue may be skipped, a piece of music may loop for an hour.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — Variability in game music"}
An exploration game uses one piece of music in three layers: a calm melody,
a percussion layer and a tense string layer.

1. When the player explores, only the melody plays.
2. When an enemy comes near, the game adds the percussion layer.
3. During a fight all three layers play. The *same* composition exists in
   several versions, chosen by the game state — variability in practice.
:::

## 1.3 The game as a composite medium

A game combines every type of digital media with something that no other
medium has: rules that the player acts upon. Jesse Schell describes a game as
four basic elements, which he calls the **elemental tetrad** (@fig-tetrad):

- **mechanics** — the procedures and rules: what the player can do and what
  happens as a result;
- **story** — the sequence of events that unfolds in the game, whether
  written in advance or emerging from play;
- **aesthetics** — how the game looks, sounds and feels: the element that the
  player perceives most directly;
- **technology** — the materials and systems that make the game possible: the
  device, the engine, the screen and the speakers.

![The elemental tetrad (after Schell). The aesthetics are the most visible element and the technology the least visible; all four together produce the player's experience.](images/tetrad.png){#fig-tetrad width=62%}

None of the four is more important than the others; each supports and limits
the rest. Schell's central point is that the designer does not create the
game for its own sake but to produce an **experience** in the player. The
media studied in this course — story, image, sound and video — live mainly in
the elements of story and aesthetics, and they are limited by technology:
memory, storage, processing power and the size of the screen.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.2 — The aim of game media"}
The media of a game succeed when they strengthen the intended **player
experience**. A beautiful image or a powerful piece of music that does not
fit the experience is a failure of design, not a success of art.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — The tetrad of a small mobile game"}
*Lantern Keeper* is a mobile game in which the player guides a small lantern
spirit through a dark forest.

1. **Mechanics**: tap to float upward; the lantern's light shrinks with time
   and grows when the player collects fireflies.
2. **Story**: the spirit must relight the lanterns of a village before
   sunrise.
3. **Aesthetics**: warm light in a cold blue forest; soft piano music; a gentle
   chime for each firefly.
4. **Technology**: a phone screen in portrait orientation; the engine draws
   the light with a cheap shader so that old phones keep 60 fps.
5. The intended experience — lonely but hopeful — is produced by all four
   together. Replacing the piano with loud rock music would break it, even
   though the mechanics would not change.
:::

![A screen of *Lantern Keeper*. Light, colour and music carry the intended experience as much as the rules do.](images/lantern-keeper.png){#fig-lantern width=40%}

The mini-game below demonstrates this last point. The mechanics never change
— tap to jump over obstacles — but the media layers can be switched on one by
one: sound effects, music, particles, camera shake and a line of story. The
same rules produce a very different experience.

{{< sim file="sims/juice-it.html" poster="sims/juice-it.png" title="Juice It: same mechanics, different media" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Confusing *aesthetics* with *graphics*. In Schell's sense, aesthetics include
sound, music, the feel of vibration and the rhythm of animation — every part
of the game that reaches the player's senses.
:::

## 1.4 The creative production pipeline

Game media are not produced in one step. Professional teams follow a
**production pipeline** of three broad stages (@fig-pipeline):

- **pre-production** — planning: the concept, the story premise, the script,
  the storyboard, the style guide that fixes colours and shapes, and the
  schedule and budget;
- **production** — making the **assets**: drawing sprites and textures,
  modelling and animating characters, composing music, recording voices and
  sound effects, capturing and editing video;
- **post-production** — finishing: editing, mixing and mastering the audio,
  colour correction, compression and export in the formats the engine needs,
  followed by integration into the game and testing.

![The creative production pipeline. Each stage produces documents or assets that the next stage uses; testing often sends work back to an earlier stage.](images/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=94%}

| Asset type | Typical formats | Example tools |
|---|---|---|
| images, sprites, textures | PNG, JPEG, PSD, SVG | Krita, GIMP, Photoshop, Figma |
| 3D models and animation | FBX, glTF, OBJ | Blender, Maya |
| music and sound effects | WAV (editing), Ogg, MP3 (game) | Audacity, Reaper, FL Studio |
| video | MP4 (H.264), MOV | DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro |
| script and storyboard | text documents, panels | word processors, storyboard tools |

: Common game assets, formats and tools. {#tbl-assets}

The pipeline also explains the structure of this course: story and
screenwriting (weeks 2–4) and storyboards (weeks 5–6) belong to
pre-production; sound, music and video (weeks 7–12) to production and
post-production; intellectual property (weeks 13–14) applies to every asset
at every stage, because every image, sound and text has an owner whose rights
must be respected.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.4 — Following one asset through the pipeline"}
The "firefly collected" sound of *Lantern Keeper*:

1. **Pre-production**: the sound design document asks for "a soft, bright
   chime, under 0.5 s, that never becomes annoying".
2. **Production**: the sound designer records a small glass bell and creates
   three variations, so that the sound does not repeat identically.
3. **Post-production**: the recordings are trimmed, their loudness is matched,
   and they are exported as compressed Ogg files.
4. **Integration and testing**: the programmer plays a random variation on
   every pickup; a tester reports that the chime is too loud next to the
   music, and the sound returns to post-production for a new mix.
:::

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses*, 3rd ed., chapters on the
designer, the experience and the game, and on the elements that make up a
game (the elemental tetrad).

## Exercises

1. Name the six types of digital media in games and give one example of each
   from a game you know.
2. Explain the two steps of digitization in your own words.
3. How many bits per second does uncompressed mono audio at 48 000 samples per
   second and 16 bits per sample need? How many kilobytes for 10 seconds?
4. How many bytes does an uncompressed $1280 \times 720$ image with 24-bit
   colour need?
5. A game logo must appear on a small app icon and on a large poster. Should
   it be stored as raster or as vector graphics? Explain.
6. Choose two of Manovich's properties and give a game example for each.
7. Name the four elements of the elemental tetrad and describe them for
   *Lantern Keeper*, using your own words.
8. Explain why "aesthetics" is not the same as "graphics".
9. Place each task in the stage of the pipeline: writing the script; mixing the
   music; recording a voice; drawing the storyboard; exporting a trailer.
10. Explain why intellectual property concerns every stage of the pipeline.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Text (subtitles), images (sprites), audio (music), video (cut-scene), animation (a walk cycle), interactive media (the game itself).
2. Sampling measures the signal at regular intervals; quantization rounds each measurement to a fixed set of levels.
3. $48\,000 \times 16 = 768\,000$ bits per second $= 96$ KB per second; 960 KB for 10 s.
4. $1280 \times 720 \times 3 = 2\,764\,800$ bytes ≈ 2.8 MB.
5. Vector: it can be drawn sharply at any size.
6. For example: modularity — levels built from reusable tiles; variability — adaptive music or translated versions.
7. Mechanics (float, collect fireflies, shrinking light), story (relight the village before sunrise), aesthetics (warm light, piano, chimes), technology (portrait phone, cheap light shader).
8. Aesthetics include everything the senses perceive — sound, music, vibration, rhythm — not only images.
9. Pre-production: script, storyboard; production: recording a voice; post-production: mixing the music, exporting a trailer.
10. Every asset — text, image, sound, video — has an owner; using or changing it at any stage requires the right to do so.
:::
